web_evidence.title: Surviving marriage narratively: Storytelling through women's friendships in Mary McCarthy's The Group (1963) and its adaptation by Lara Feigel (2020)
web_evidence.note: Peer-reviewed structural analysis identifies McCarthy's controlling voice as omniscient and the chapters as free-indirect narration from shifting characters' viewpoints. It also analyzes the novel's generalizing “you” as locally ambiguous character-oriented discourse, not sustained second-person narration.

person_note: The controlling narrator is nonparticipating and third person, moving among the women's perspectives through omniscient or close free-indirect narration. Sustained quote passages corroborate this structure. First-person forms occur in character speech, while recurring “you” forms are generic generalizations within dialogue or free-indirect thought rather than a story-specific protagonist addressed as “you.” The choral Group voice is likewise described by whole-book sources as a distinctive third-person collective voice, not a separate first-person strand. Two clipped quotes remain locally unresolved, but they do not create credible book-level conflict.
